content.text: Your app's database user, container user and service account aren't used only by your code. They're used by every bug in it, and by anyone who gets its credentials. Give the running app only the rights it uses at run time, move schema changes to a separate deployment identity, run containers as non-root, and scope service accounts to what the workload calls.

A penetration test finds a SQL injection in an old reporting endpoint. That alone would be a serious finding, but the report rates it critical: through that one parameter, the tester dropped the audit log table and added a new user to
db_owner
. The API's login was a member of
db_owner
because the app applies EF Core migrations at startup. In the review meeting, the tech lead's first reaction is: "But only our code uses that login."
The common misconception
The belief: the app's own database user or service account can safely have admin rights, because only our code uses it.

It sounds reasonable. The credentials are secret, no person logs in with them, and the code is yours and reviewed. Admin rights also remove a whole class of production surprises: no "permission denied" when a new feature needs a table, and
Database.Migrate()
at startup just works. Restricting the app looks like friction with no attacker in sight.
The flaw is in "only our code". Code with a bug in it is still your code, and it runs with exactly the rights you gave it.
What actually happens
Every bug inherits the app's rights
An injection, an
SSRF

, a vulnerable dependency or a leaked connection string all end the same way: someone else's instructions run under your app's identity. Parameterized queries, covered earlier in this path, stop the injection itself.
Least privilege
decides what happens when something slips through anyway.

OWASP's Database Security Cheat Sheet states the rule for app accounts: they "should only have the minimal permissions required for the application to function". It is specific: "Do not use the built-in root, sa or SYS accounts", "Do not grant the account administrative rights over the database instance", and the account "should not be the owner of the database as this can lead to privilege escalation vulnerabilities." It also says each account should be "Used by a single application or service."
Running and deploying need different rights

Most apps get admin rights for one reason: schema changes. Microsoft's EF Core docs are direct about it: "Use a separate identity for deployment that has permission to change the schema. The identity used by the application at run time should normally have only the permissions the application needs to read and write data." On migrating at startup, they list the cost: "The application must have elevated access to modify the database schema." A
migration bundle
or SQL script run by the pipeline, with its own login, removes that need.
Root in a container is still root

Containers have identities too. OWASP's Docker Security Cheat Sheet calls running as an unprivileged user "the best way to prevent privilege escalation attacks", and reminds you that even with rootless Docker "the shared kernel remains part of the security boundary", the point the article "Docker Is Not a VM" makes. .NET's Linux images ship a non-root user named
app
, but you opt in. Microsoft's .NET 8 notes say: "To run as non-root, add the following line at the end of your Dockerfile", and expose its UID as
APP_UID
for Kubernetes'
runAsNonRoot
check.
A service account is a login to your cluster
In Kubernetes, the pod's
service account
is the app's identity for the API server. The RBAC Good Practices page says "minimal RBAC rights should be assigned to users and service accounts", recommends namespaced
RoleBindings
over
ClusterRoleBindings
, warns against wildcards, which also grant "all object types which are created in the future", and suggests
automountServiceAccountToken: false
for pods that never call the API.
Two database identities, on a real SQL Server

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: We ran both setups on a throwaway database in SQL Server 2022, then sent the tester's statements as each login. As a
db_owner
member, all of them succeeded: the audit table was gone, a
Payload
table appeared, and a new user
helper
sat in
db_owner
. As the least-privilege app login:
The app still reads and writes its data, so features keep working. The migrator login created a table, altered
Orders
and wrote its history row, but it couldn't create users either. The containers get the same treatment in the final stage of the Dockerfile:

blocks.code:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/publish .
USER $APP_UID
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "Shop.Api.dll"]

rows.text: A separate login with DDL rights, used only by the pipeline

content.text: An attacker who reaches your database through the app doesn't need your password. With
db_owner
, they can also leave a door open: our test added a user to
db_owner
in one statement. With DML-only rights, the same statement failed.

blocks.title: Read access to every table is still a lot

content.text: SELECT

on the whole schema lets an injection read every table the app can. For sensitive data, OWASP lists finer levels: "Table-level permissions", "Column-level permissions", "Row-level permissions", and access through restricted views.

blocks.title: Find your over-privileged identities in one query

content.text: SELECT USER_NAME(member_principal_id) FROM sys.database_role_members WHERE role_principal_id = DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID('db_owner');
lists every
db_owner
member. Any login your app uses at run time shouldn't be on that list.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: List every identity the app runs as

content.text: Database logins, cloud and Kubernetes service accounts, the container user and API keys to other services. Write down what each one is granted today.
Apply migrations from the pipeline with a bundle or a reviewed script, under a separate login. Remove
Migrate()
from startup and drop the app's DDL rights.

items.title: Grant the app what it uses

content.text: Start with data rights on the app's schema. Tighten tables that hold sensitive data with column or row rules, or put them behind views.
Add
USER $APP_UID
to .NET images and set
runAsNonRoot
in the pod's security context. Keep the default port 8080: Microsoft notes that moving back to port 80 means "you can't run as non-root."

items.title: Scope service accounts and review them

content.text: Disable token mounting where the pod never calls the API, bind namespaced roles with explicit verbs, and review grants regularly, as both OWASP and Kubernetes advise.
Key takeaways

items.text: The app's identity is used by every bug in the app, not just by the code you meant to run.
Give the running app data rights only; never
Run migrations from the pipeline with a separate login, so startup doesn't need DDL rights.
Containers should run as a non-root user; .NET images ship one you opt into with
Give service accounts namespaced, explicit permissions, and no token when they don't call the API.
